title: Getting paid, and clocking off
subtitle: Minimum wage, unlawful deductions and working time limits
objectives: State the National Minimum Wage/National Living Wage framework and identify who is entitled to it
Apply the s 13 ERA 1996 restriction on unlawful deductions from wages to a new fact pattern, including its exceptions
Explain the core Working Time Regulations 1998 protections and apply the Harpur Trust calendar-week method for a part-year worker's holiday pay

leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes a statutory floor on hourly pay for workers, enforced by HMRC
Prohibits a deduction from wages unless statutorily authorised, contractually authorised in advance, or consented to in writing
Sets the 48-hour average working week, daily and weekly rest, rest breaks, and 5.6 weeks' paid annual leave
Part-year workers' statutory holiday pay must be calculated by the calendar-week averaging method, not pro-rated by a percentage such as 12.07%

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is the floor beneath almost every worker, not just employees — the protections in this lesson attach to worker status from Lesson 1, and most of them cannot be contracted out of. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the numbers — this lesson checks whether you can run the calculation on an odd fact pattern.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards worked calculations and scenario questions: expect numbers to check, not just rules to recite.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the minimum wage and deduction rules are the foundation the working time material in the later parts builds on.

overview.hook: A term-time-only music teacher, paid only for the weeks she actually worked, was given a smaller slice of holiday pay than a colleague who worked all year round — calculated, her employer said, fairly and proportionately. The Supreme Court disagreed, and in doing so overturned a method of calculating holiday pay that thousands of employers had used for years. This lesson is about the statutory floor under every worker's pay packet, and the one arithmetic trap that catches out even well-advised employers.

parts.heading: The wage floor: National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage
parts.voice: structural — sets out the framework before the detail
body: The National Minimum Wage Act 1998 sets a statutory floor beneath what any worker can be paid per hour, enforced not just through employment tribunals but through HMRC, which can issue a notice of underpayment, impose a penalty, and name and shame non-compliant employers. This is a worker right, not an employee-only right — it follows the wider s 230(3)(b) ERA 1996 definition from Lesson 1, so genuinely self-employed contractors fall outside it, but employees and limb (b) workers alike are covered.

The Act itself sets the framework and the enforcement machinery; the actual rates are set by regulations updated annually, with the highest rate — the National Living Wage — applying to workers aged 21 and over, and lower age-banded rates for younger workers and apprentices. A worker cannot contract out of the minimum wage: an agreement to be paid less, however freely entered into, is simply unenforceable to that extent, and the employer remains liable to make up the shortfall.

Two calculation traps recur in practice and in exams alike: unpaid working time (time spent travelling between assignments, or on-call time where the worker cannot genuinely use the time freely) can count towards minimum wage hours even though it isn't separately paid, and certain deductions — for uniform, or tools required for the job — can reduce a worker's effective hourly rate below the minimum even where the payslip shows a compliant hourly figure.

components.definition: The highest banding of the National Minimum Wage, applying to workers aged 21 and over, set annually by regulations under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 and enforceable by HMRC as well as through the employment tribunal.

interaction.prompt: Does the National Minimum Wage apply to workers, or only to employees?
options: Workers generally, following the s 230(3)(b) ERA 1996 definition — not just employees
Employees only
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Minimum wage protection follows the broader worker definition, so limb (b) workers are covered even though they can't claim unfair dismissal.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — this is a worker right, following the wider s 230(3)(b) definition from Lesson 1, not an employee-only right.

parts.heading: Section 13 ERA 1996: when a deduction is lawful
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Section 13 ERA 1996 protects workers against unauthorised deductions from wages — a protection that matters just as much for how narrow its exceptions are as for the general rule itself. The default position is that an employer may not deduct anything from a worker's wages at all.

There are only two routes to a lawful deduction: the deduction is required or authorised by a statutory provision (such as PAYE income tax or National Insurance) or a relevant provision of the worker's contract that the worker has been shown a copy of, or notified of in writing, in advance of the deduction being made — or the worker has previously signified their agreement or consent to the deduction in writing. Retrospective consent, after the deduction has already been taken, does not satisfy this second route; the consent or contractual authorisation has to exist before the deduction is made.

A separate, additional layer of protection applies to deductions from retail workers' wages for cash shortages or stock deficiencies, capping any single deduction at 10% of the gross wages payable on that pay day — a rule aimed squarely at the historic practice of employers passing on till discrepancies or shrinkage to shop-floor staff.

components.text: An employer shall not make a deduction from wages of a worker employed by him unless— (a) the deduction is required or authorised to be made by virtue of a statutory provision or a relevant provision of the worker's contract, or (b) the worker has previously signified in writing his agreement or consent to the making of the deduction.
elements: Default rule: no deduction without lawful authority
Route (a) — statutory authority, or a contractual term notified in advance
Route (b) — the worker's prior written consent, given before the deduction is made

interaction.prompt: Under s 13 ERA 1996, which of these satisfies the requirement for a lawful deduction?
options: A worker signs a form consenting to a deduction the day after it has already been taken from their wages
A worker's contract, shown to them before the deduction is made, contains a clause authorising deductions for till shortages
An employer verbally tells a worker a deduction is coming, with no written record at all
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A contractual term the worker was notified of in advance satisfies route (a). Retrospective consent and unrecorded verbal notice both fail the statutory requirements.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at timing and form. The consent or contractual authority has to exist, in an appropriate written or notified form, before the deduction is made — retrospective sign-off and undocumented verbal notice both fail.

parts.heading: The 48-hour week and the daily rhythm of rest
parts.voice: structural — a checklist students will return to
body: The Working Time Regulations 1998 implement the EU Working Time Directive into domestic law and set out the core limits on how long, and how continuously, a worker can be required to work. The headline rule is the 48-hour average working week: a worker's working time, averaged over a 17-week reference period, must not normally exceed 48 hours. Crucially, a worker can individually opt out of the 48-hour limit by a specific, freely given written agreement — this is a genuine, exercisable opt-out, not something the employer can impose by default or bury in a standard contract without the worker's separate written agreement.

Underneath the weekly limit sit daily and weekly rest requirements: a worker is entitled to 11 consecutive hours of rest in each 24-hour period, and either 24 hours of uninterrupted rest in each 7-day period or 48 hours in each 14-day period. Where a working day is longer than six hours, the worker is entitled to an uninterrupted rest break of at least 20 minutes, away from their workstation.

These are minimum floors, not typical arrangements — many contracts provide more generous rest than the Regulations require. But where a dispute arises about whether a working pattern is lawful, these are the numbers to check first, before looking at anything the contract itself says.

components.label: Working Time Regulations 1998 — the core limits
points: 48-hour average working week, over a 17-week reference period, subject to a genuine individual opt-out
11 consecutive hours' daily rest in each 24-hour period
24 hours' weekly rest in each 7-day period (or 48 hours in each 14 days)
A 20-minute uninterrupted rest break where the working day exceeds 6 hours

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that breaches the Working Time Regulations' daily rest requirement.
interaction.scenarioText: Ollie finishes his evening shift at 11pm and is rostered to start his next shift at 6am the following morning — a gap of just seven hours before he is due back at work.
tappableSpans: rostered to start his next shift at 6am
a gap of just seven hours
interaction.correctSpan: a gap of just seven hours
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The Regulations require 11 consecutive hours' rest in each 24-hour period; a seven-hour gap falls well short and breaches that minimum, whatever the individual shift times happen to be.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The individual shift times aren't the issue on their own — what matters is the length of the rest period between them, and seven hours is less than the 11-hour minimum the Regulations require.

parts.heading: 5.6 weeks, and how a 'week's pay' is worked out
parts.voice: direct — moves quickly from entitlement to the harder question of calculation
body: Every worker is entitled to 5.6 weeks of paid annual leave a year — for a worker on a standard five-day week, this works out to 28 days, made up of the 4 weeks required by the original EU Working Time Directive plus an additional 1.6 weeks added by domestic regulations. This entitlement cannot be replaced by a payment in lieu except on termination of employment; a worker cannot simply choose to work through their whole holiday entitlement in exchange for extra pay while still employed.

The genuinely hard question, for a worker whose hours or pay vary, is what a 'week's pay' actually means for holiday pay purposes. For a worker with no normal working hours or variable pay, the calculation looks back over a reference period — the 52 weeks before the leave is taken, counting only weeks in which the worker actually earned something (skipping back further to find 52 such weeks if any given week produced no pay) — and averages pay across those weeks.

This reference-period, averaging approach sounds mechanical, but it produces genuinely counter-intuitive results once you apply it to workers who don't work a standard, regular pattern — which is exactly the problem the next case in this lesson had to resolve.

components.definition: For a worker without normal, regular working hours, statutory holiday pay is calculated by averaging pay over the 52 weeks in which the worker actually earned pay before the leave is taken — skipping back further than 52 weeks where necessary to find that many paid weeks, rather than counting every calendar week regardless of whether it was worked.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a worker can be paid extra in lieu of taking their statutory annual leave while remaining in employment?
sliderLabels: Confident this is not permitted, except on termination
interaction.correctPosition: Confident this is not permitted, except on termination
interaction.explanation: Statutory annual leave exists to secure actual rest, not simply extra pay — a payment in lieu of taking it is only permitted when the employment ends, not as a standing alternative during ongoing employment.

parts.heading: Harpur Trust v Brazel: the part-year worker's holiday pay
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before drawing out the doctrine
body: Lesley Brazel was a visiting music teacher at a school, engaged on a permanent contract but working only during term time — roughly 32 to 35 weeks a year, with no work, and no pay, during the school holidays. The school calculated her holiday pay using a method widely used across the education sector and recommended in Acas guidance: 12.07% of her annual pay, on the reasoning that 5.6 weeks is 12.07% of the 46.4 working weeks in a standard full-time year, and that a part-year worker's holiday pay should be pro-rated down to reflect how much of the year they actually worked.

The Supreme Court held this was wrong. Lady Rose's judgment worked directly from the statutory language: the Working Time Regulations and ERA 1996 give every worker 5.6 weeks of leave — full stop, not pro-rated by reference to how many weeks of the year they work — and calculate a week's pay for holiday purposes using the 52-week averaging reference period, counting only weeks actually worked and skipping weeks with no pay. Neither the Regulations nor the Directive contain any pro-rating mechanism for part-year workers; the 12.07% method was a practical convention, not a rule grounded in the statutory text.

The consequence, acknowledged and accepted by the Court, is that a part-year worker like Brazel can end up with proportionally more generous holiday pay, as a percentage of annual earnings, than a full-time comparator — because the calculation counts only the weeks she was actually paid, ignoring the unpaid weeks entirely, while still crediting her with the full 5.6 weeks everyone else gets. That result looked anomalous to the school, but the Court held that following the plain statutory method, even to a counter-intuitive outcome for part-year workers, was preferable to grafting on an unwritten pro-rating principle the legislation simply does not contain.

components.factsShort: A term-time-only music teacher on a permanent contract had her holiday pay calculated at 12.07% of annual earnings; she argued the statutory 52-week averaging method should apply instead, uncapped by any pro-rating.
components.ratioShort: Statutory holiday pay for a part-year worker on a permanent contract must be calculated using the 52-week reference-period averaging method, giving the full 5.6 weeks' leave with no pro-rating for weeks not worked.

expanded.facts: Brazel worked as a visiting music teacher under a permanent, year-round contract, but only actually taught during school term time, roughly 32–35 weeks a year, receiving no pay during the school holidays. The school's payroll provider calculated her holiday pay at 12.07% of the pay she earned in each term, following the standard 'Acas method' used widely for part-year and casual staff.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lady Rose held that the statutory scheme gives every worker, including a part-year worker on a permanent contract, an entitlement to 5.6 weeks' leave, calculated using the 52-week reference period defined in the (then) amended ERA 1996 provisions on a week's pay — a method that does not pro-rate down for weeks not worked, and that neither the Working Time Regulations nor the Working Time Directive contain any requirement or mechanism to do so.
expanded.significance: This is the leading modern authority on holiday pay calculation for part-year and irregular-hours workers. It rejected a widely used industry practice (the 12.07% method) as inconsistent with the statutory wording, even though it accepted the result could look disproportionately generous for genuinely part-year workers compared with full-time equivalents.

interaction.prompt: In the extract below, highlight the sentence that states the ratio of Harpur Trust v Brazel.
interaction.passage: The statutory scheme gives every worker an entitlement to 5.6 weeks' leave. For a worker without normal working hours, a week's pay is calculated using the 52-week reference period, counting only weeks actually paid. Neither the Regulations nor the Directive contain any mechanism requiring that entitlement to be pro-rated down according to the proportion of the year actually worked, and none should be read in.
interaction.ratioSentence: Neither the Regulations nor the Directive contain any mechanism requiring that entitlement to be pro-rated down according to the proportion of the year actually worked, and none should be read in.

testPool.prompt: Which statute sets the enforceable statutory floor on hourly pay in the UK, and who enforces it?
acceptableAnswers: National Minimum Wage Act 1998, enforced by HMRC
testPool.modelAnswer: The National Minimum Wage Act 1998, enforced by HMRC as well as through the employment tribunal.

testPool.prompt: Name the two routes under s 13 ERA 1996 by which a deduction from wages can be lawful.
acceptableAnswers: statutory authority or a contractual provision notified in advance, or the worker's prior written consent
statutory/contractual authority, or prior written consent
testPool.modelAnswer: (a) A statutory provision or a relevant contractual provision the worker was notified of in advance; or (b) the worker's prior written consent, given before the deduction is made.

testPool.prompt: Can a worker individually opt out of the 48-hour average working week limit under the Working Time Regulations 1998?
options: Yes — by a specific, freely given written agreement
No — the 48-hour limit can never be varied by agreement

testPool.prompt: How many weeks of paid annual leave does the Working Time Regulations 1998 framework give a full-time worker in total?
options: 4 weeks
5.6 weeks, made up of the original 4-week EU entitlement plus an additional 1.6 weeks
6 weeks
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often recall only the original 4-week EU minimum and stop there. Domestic regulations add a further 1.6 weeks, bringing the total statutory minimum to 5.6 weeks — 28 days for a standard five-day working week.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to calculate a week's pay for holiday pay purposes under the 52-week reference period, following Harpur Trust v Brazel.
items: Look back from the date leave is taken across up to 52 weeks
Discard any week in which the worker earned no pay, and look back further to replace it
Continue until 52 paid weeks have been identified (or fewer, if the worker has not worked that long)
Average the pay across those weeks to produce the week's pay figure

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a tribunal checks when assessing whether a deduction from wages was lawful under s 13 ERA 1996.
items: Identify that a deduction has in fact been made from wages
Check whether it is authorised by statute or by a contractual term notified in advance
If not, check whether the worker gave written consent before the deduction was made
If neither route applies, treat the deduction as unlawful

testPool.prompt: Under the Working Time Regulations 1998, what is the minimum uninterrupted daily rest a worker is entitled to in each 24-hour period?
options: 8 consecutive hours
11 consecutive hours
24 consecutive hours

testPool.prompt: Which of these deductions is lawful under s 13 ERA 1996?
testPool.scenarioA: An employer deducts £50 from a shop worker's wages for a till shortage that occurred that week, relying on a clause the worker was shown and signed before starting the job, and the deduction does not exceed 10% of that pay day's gross wages.
testPool.scenarioB: An employer deducts £50 from a warehouse worker's wages for a damaged pallet, with no contractual term authorising it and no consent obtained from the worker at any point, before or after.
testPool.explanation: A satisfies s 13: a contractual term notified in advance, plus (for a retail worker) compliance with the 10% cash-shortage cap. B has no statutory or contractual authority and no consent at all, so it is an unlawful deduction.

testPool.prompt: Which worker's holiday pay should be calculated using the full, uncapped 52-week averaging method from Harpur Trust v Brazel, rather than a pro-rated percentage method?
testPool.scenarioA: A permanent employee who works only during school term time, paid only for the weeks she actually teaches, with no pay during the holidays.
testPool.scenarioB: A genuinely casual worker engaged separately for each individual assignment under a series of entirely distinct short-term contracts, with no umbrella or permanent contract linking them.
testPool.explanation: Harpur Trust concerned a worker on a single, continuous, permanent contract who simply didn't work every week of the year — exactly A's position. B raises a different and separate question about whether successive short engagements even amount to one continuous contract at all, which the case did not resolve.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this payslip scenario that most clearly breaches the National Minimum Wage.
testPool.scenarioText: Sam is paid exactly the adult minimum hourly rate for every hour recorded on his rota. Separately, his employer deducts the cost of a compulsory uniform from his wages each month, bringing his actual effective hourly pay, once the deduction is accounted for, below the statutory minimum.
tappableSpans: paid exactly the adult minimum hourly rate
for every hour recorded on his rota
deducts the cost of a compulsory uniform
bringing his actual effective hourly pay, once the deduction is accounted for, below the statutory minimum
testPool.correctSpan: bringing his actual effective hourly pay, once the deduction is accounted for, below the statutory minimum
testPool.explanation: A payslip that shows a compliant hourly rate can still breach the minimum wage once a deduction for something required for the job — like a compulsory uniform — is taken into account, because what matters is the effective rate actually received, not the headline figure.

testPool.prompt: A casual worker earns £400 in week 1, nothing in week 2 (no shifts offered), and £350 in week 3, then takes a day's leave. Under the 52-week reference period method, which weeks are used to calculate her week's pay?
options: All three weeks, including week 2, averaged together
Only weeks 1 and 3 — week 2 is discarded because no pay was earned, and the calculation looks back further to find enough paid weeks
Only the most recent week (week 3)
testPool.explanation: The 52-week reference period counts only weeks in which pay was actually earned, skipping any week with no pay and looking back further to find the required number of paid weeks — it does not average in unpaid weeks as zeros.

testPool.prompt: A school uses the 12.07% method to calculate holiday pay for its term-time-only staff on permanent contracts, exactly as Harpur Trust did before losing its case. Is this method now safe to rely on?
options: Yes — the Supreme Court approved the 12.07% method for all part-year workers
No — the Supreme Court held the correct method is the 52-week reference-period average, giving 5.6 weeks' leave without any pro-rating by the proportion of the year worked
It depends on whether the worker is under 21
testPool.explanation: Harpur Trust v Brazel rejected the 12.07% method as inconsistent with the statutory wording for a worker on a permanent, continuous contract who simply doesn't work every week — the correct method is the uncapped 52-week average.

testPool.prompt: Priya is employed on a permanent, year-round contract as an exam invigilator but is only actually called on to work, and paid, during exam periods — roughly 12 weeks a year. Her employer calculates her holiday pay as 12.07% of her annual earnings, arguing that giving her the full 5.6 weeks at the 52-week average rate would be disproportionate to how little of the year she works. Analyse whether the employer's approach is lawful.
factsToOrder: Priya is on a permanent, continuous contract
She is only called on to work, and paid, during exam periods (roughly 12 weeks a year)
Her employer uses the 12.07% method to calculate holiday pay
The employer argues the full 52-week average method would be disproportionate

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the employer may lawfully calculate a part-year worker's statutory holiday pay using the 12.07% method rather than the 52-week reference-period average.
modelAnswer.rule: Following Harpur Trust v Brazel, a worker on a permanent, continuous contract is entitled to the full 5.6 weeks' statutory leave, calculated using the 52-week reference-period averaging method (counting only weeks actually paid); neither the Working Time Regulations nor the Working Time Directive permit pro-rating that entitlement down by reference to the proportion of the year actually worked, however disproportionate the result may appear.
modelAnswer.application: Priya's position mirrors Brazel's directly: a single, continuous, permanent contract under which she is paid only for the weeks she actually works. The employer's disproportionality argument is the same argument the school made and lost in Harpur Trust — the statutory language simply contains no pro-rating mechanism, however counter-intuitive the resulting figure.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The employer's 12.07% method is unlawful; Priya's holiday pay must be calculated using the uncapped 52-week reference-period average, giving her the full 5.6 weeks' entitlement.

testPool.prompt: The Supreme Court in Harpur Trust v Brazel accepted that its ruling could give part-year workers proportionally more generous holiday pay than full-time comparators. Why did that not change the outcome?
options: Because the Court considered the statutory wording gave no basis for pro-rating and declined to read in a mechanism the legislation does not contain, even though the result looked anomalous
Because full-time workers were found to be unfairly advantaged in other, unrelated ways that balanced it out
Because the anomaly only affects workers earning above a certain salary threshold
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to assume a court would soften an odd-looking result through some unstated fairness adjustment. Lady Rose's judgment is explicit that the statutory text simply does not contain a pro-rating mechanism, and that following it faithfully — even to a result that looks disproportionate on the facts of a particular case — was preferable to inventing one.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is assuming a headline compliant figure — an hourly rate, a written consent clause, a familiar percentage-based calculation — settles the question on its own. Check the effective rate after deductions, the timing of consent, and, for holiday pay, whether the statutory reference-period method has actually been used rather than a pro-rating shortcut.
